Fleet-Marine response teams deployed to flooded areas in Rizal

NAVAL STATION JOSE ANDRADA, Manila – Disaster Relief and Response Teams (DRRT) from the fleet and marine units of the Philippine Navy are deployed to Rizal which also suffered heavy flooding due to Typhoon 'Ulysses'.
 
Two DRRTs from Fleet-Marine Ready Force and three Amphibious Assault Vehicles (AAVs) from the Philippine Marine Corps (PMC) are being utilized for rescue operations in Rizal. Another AAV is on standby and ready for rapid deployment.

The teams made coordination with the officer-in-charge of the Incident Command and Management Center in Montalban Rodriguez Municipal Hall prior to their deployment to affected barangays. 

Primarily used in combat operations by PMC, AAVs are also useful during the conduct of humanitarian assistance and disaster response (HADR) operations. Each AAV can accommodate up to twenty passengers and can maneuver through deep water or flood in this instance.

Meanwhile, another amphibian truck from the Naval Affiliated Reserve Force-NCR is also mobilized to assist in the aforesaid operations. 

This deployment is part of the Navy's ongoing efforts to assist other government agencies in responding to our fellow Filipinos being affected by the widespread flooding in Mega Manila triggered by 'Ulysses'.

(Source: Philippine Navy)

Our friends at Bad Student lost everything in #UlyssesPH. Their risograph machines, drum inks, workstations, and archive of art prints were irretrievably lost as floodwaters inundated their studio and living space. They had to swim several hours to safety, but thankfully are now safe. 

The Philippines is the country at greatest risk of climate crisis, and we are set to face more typhoons before the year ends. As wealthier nations and big corporations destroy our environment with impunity, we Filipinos bear the brunt, living under the constant threat of disasters both natural and man-made. Our creative practices are not spared. We need justice.

Bad Student is the first riso art studio in the country, and was set to represent the Philippines in the upcoming TOKYO ART BOOK FAIR / VIRTUAL ART BOOK FAIR. They have continuously supported emerging talents through workshops, grants, and collaborations, and highlight Filipino culture in their projects. 

Amid a deluge of digital experiences, their promotion of riso as a venue for artistic exploration has helped renew interest in print design, printmaking, and tactile analog formats among young people in our creative community.

Flooded Car? Here's what to do. ✅❎

1. Immediately disconnect the negative cable of your car battery to avoid any possible short circuit. This is also to protect the ECU or computer box from damage.

2. Do not start the engine. Try to push the car out to higher ground or try jacking it with the car jack.

3. Disengage and release the parking brake. Keep the transmission in 1st gear (for manual transmission) or "P" (for automatic transmission) to prevent the brake canvas from sticking. This is even more important for cars that use drum brakes.

4. Take plenty of photos both inside and outside the car to document any damage or how deep the car was underwater. This will be useful for both the Insurance and/or Professional Mechanic to determine the extent of the damage.

5. Wait at least 24 hours before you do anything to the vehicle, giving it time to drain, if not completely dry out.

6. If the water got so deep that the dashboard was covered, do not try to start it at all. If any liquid is in the cylinders it will cause damage to the engine. Most of the electronics in the car would have been submerged at this depth, as well.

7. If you don’t think the water got that high, it’s still best to take a look at the oil dipstick to see if there are any traces of water in the lubrication system. If so, assume the engine is flooded and don’t try to start it.

8. You’re in better shape if the water stayed below the center line of your wheels. Nevertheless, let the interior air out as much as possible before trying to start it, taking out the floor mats, trunk mat and even the seats. Much of the wiring and some of the computers in today’s cars are located under the carpet and console box, so even if the engine compartment was not inundated, you could still experience faults to secondary systems.

9. When in doubt, either have your vehicle towed to your trusted service center or call your professional mechanic/electrician for a more thorough inspection and assessment.

Rescue ops ongoing

Marikina residents in the early morning of Thursday called for help as the flood already reached the third floor of their homes.

Flooded Car? Here's what to do:

1. Immediately disconnect the negative cable of your car battery to avoid any possible short circuit. This is also to protect the ECU or computer box from damage.

2. Do not start the engine. Try to push the car out to higher ground or try jacking it with the car jack.

3. Disengage and release the parking brake. Keep the transmission in 1st gear (for manual transmission) or "P" (for automatic transmission) to prevent the brake canvas from sticking. This is even more important for cars that use drum brakes.

4. Take plenty of photos both inside and outside the car to document any damage or how deep the car was underwater. This will be useful for both the Insurance and/or Professional Mechanic to determine the extent of the damage.

5. Wait at least 24 hours before you do anything to the vehicle, giving it time to drain, if not completely dry out.

6. If the water got so deep that the dashboard was covered, do not try to start it at all. If any liquid is in the cylinders it will cause damage to the engine. Most of the electronics in the car would have been submerged at this depth, as well.

7. If you don’t think the water got that high, it’s still best to take a look at the oil dipstick to see if there are any traces of water in the lubrication system. If so, assume the engine is flooded and don’t try to start it.

8. You’re in better shape if the water stayed below the center line of your wheels. Nevertheless, let the interior air out as much as possible before trying to start it, taking out the floor mats, trunk mat and even the seats. Much of the wiring and some of the computers in today’s cars are located under the carpet and console box, so even if the engine compartment was not inundated, you could still experience faults to secondary systems.

9. When in doubt, either have your vehicle towed to your trusted service center or call your professional mechanic/electrician for a more thorough inspection and assessment.

1. Immediately disconnect the negative cable of your car battery to avoid any possible short circuit. This is also to protect the ECU or computer box from damage.

2. Do not start the engine. Try to push the car out to higher ground or try jacking it with the car jack.

3. Disengage and release the parking brake. Keep the transmission in 1st gear (for manual transmission) or "P" (for automatic transmission) to prevent the brake canvas from sticking. This is even more important for cars that use drum brakes.

4. Take plenty of photos both inside and outside the car to document any damage or how deep the car was underwater. This will be useful for both the Insurance and/or Professional Mechanic to determine the extent of the damage.

5. Wait at least 24 hours before you do anything to the vehicle, giving it time to drain, if not completely dry out.

6. If the water got so deep that the dashboard was covered, do not try to start it at all. If any liquid is in the cylinders it will cause damage to the engine. Most of the electronics in the car would have been submerged at this depth, as well.

7. If you don’t think the water got that high, it’s still best to take a look at the oil dipstick to see if there are any traces of water in the lubrication system. If so, assume the engine is flooded and don’t try to start it.

8. You’re in better shape if the water stayed below the center line of your wheels. Nevertheless, let the interior air out as much as possible before trying to start it, taking out the floor mats, trunk mat and even the seats. Much of the wiring and some of the computers in today’s cars are located under the carpet and console box, so even if the engine compartment was not inundated, you could still experience faults to secondary systems.

9. When in doubt, either have your vehicle towed to your trusted service center or call your professional mechanic/electrician for a more thorough inspection and assessment.
